title: Call by Value
concept: When you pass a variable to a function, a ‘copy’ is passed. The original is safe.

steps.title: Start main function
steps.explanation:
The main frame is created.

The key point this time is that when you pass a regular variable to a function, a copy of the value is passed, not the original.

steps.title: Declare and initialize variable a
steps.explanation:
Prepare the original variable `a` with `int a = 10;`.

Compare this value before and after calling the function to check Call by Value operation.

steps.title: Before value output
steps.explanation: Before calling, print the value of `a` to record the reference state.

steps.title: Function calls and value copying
steps.explanation:
When calling `tryToChange(a);`, only the value of `a` is copied to parameter `x`.

`a` and `x` are separate variables in different memory spaces.

steps.title: change copy x
steps.explanation:
Changing `x=999` inside the function only changes the copy.

The original `a` is not affected.

steps.title: Function internal output
steps.explanation:
Inside the function, `x=999` is output.

This is the result of the copy value being changed.

steps.title: After output - original as is
steps.explanation:
If you print `a` after the call, it's still 10.

In Call by Value, the function cannot directly change the original variable.

quiz.explanation:
The only thing incremented is copy `n`.
The original `a` remains unchanged and remains 5.

misconceptions.wrong: If you add a variable to a function, it will be connected.
misconceptions.correct: It is not connected, but copied with ‘Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V’.
misconceptions.why:
This is the default behavior for data protection.
If you want to change it, you have to use a pointer.

keyTakeaway: If you throw a variable into a function, only the value is copied. What if you want to change the original?
